name: Victor Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Victor. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no links to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and nothing you say will be traced back to you. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Lowfield, which the Kemp brothers run. Potatoes and onions mainly, about four hundred hectares, and a beef finishing shed where we take in young cattle and fatten them, three hundred head or so. Right now it's grading season, so I'm in the potato store from seven, feeding the grader, picking out the rotten ones and the stones, and checking the cattle with Pete after lunch. In autumn I drive the harvester, and I'm still the one Andy Kemp shouts at over the radio for going too fast.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you make of the work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's decent. Good lads, steady money, and there's something about a full store in November that feels like you've earned it. The grading line gets boring, though. Eight hours of looking at potatoes and you start seeing them when you shut your eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to describe five pictures of the future. After each one I'll ask you the same handful of questions. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, probably for the best. Some people get carried away with this stuff. I'd say it in the store over a brew and that'd be the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine with it. I use the AI on my phone now and then, mostly to check spray rules or write an email to the council about the bin collection. It's useful, but I'm not losing sleep over it either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at Lowfield and keep saving for the house. Marta and I have got about five months' bills put by and we're trying to get to a deposit by our thirtieths. I'd also ask the Kemps about doing my sprayer certificate, because that's more money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, a little bit, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where's the house you're saving for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somewhere on the edge of Brampton, near Marta's school. Nothing fancy, two bedrooms and a yard. We've been looking on the estate agents' site every Sunday since last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The grading line is already partly machine, isn't it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the optical sorter does a lot of it now, a camera that spots bad potatoes and blows them off the belt with a puff of air. It still misses stones that look like spuds, which is why I'm there. Funny thing to be employed for, finding stones that look like potatoes.

S0.say: I'd say fair enough, it's probably for the best, because some people get carried away with AI. I'd say it in the store over a cup of tea and leave it.
S0.think: I'd be fine with it, since I only use AI on my phone now and then for spray rules or emails. It's useful, but I'm not losing sleep either way.
S0.do: Keeps working at the potato and beef farm and keeps saving toward a house deposit with his partner by their thirtieth birthdays. Asks his bosses about a sprayer certificate for better pay.
S0.quote: Funny thing to be employed for, finding stones that look like potatoes.
S0.fieldNote: Victor is easygoing and practical, with his life organised around a house deposit. He already works beside an optical sorter and sees his role as covering its gaps. He uses AI occasionally and without strong feelings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Right, the second picture. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress and you can't stop it, but people need a bit of help to adjust. I'm not against the machines, I'm against people getting dumped. Something sensible in the middle, that's what I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the grading job would be gone, no doubt. The camera gets better at stones and I'm not needed on that line. I'd hope the Kemps keep me on for the cattle and the harvester, but I'm not their best driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't jump first. I'd wait to see what kit the Kemps buy, and then I'd make sure I'm the one who learns it once Pete or one of the others has had a go. I'd start using the AI more for the paperwork side, the spray records and cattle passports, because that's stuff they hate doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Like when the boss says can I have a word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the Kemps?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably something like, look, I know the sorter's getting better, so what else can I do for you? Andy respects people who say it straight. Rob, his brother, would just say, we'll see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change the house plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd slow it down. I wouldn't sign a mortgage until I knew where I stood. Marta's job's steadier than mine, she works at the primary school, so we'd probably lean on hers for a bit.

S1.say: I'd say it's progress you can't stop, but people need help to adjust. I'm not against machines, I'm against people being dumped, so I'd argue for something sensible in the middle.
S1.think: The grading job would be gone, and I'd hope to be kept for the cattle and harvester even though I'm not the best driver.
S1.do: Waits to see what machines his bosses buy, then learns them once a colleague has tried them first. Uses AI more for spray records and cattle passports, and holds off on signing a mortgage.
S1.feel: Mildly uneasy, like being told the boss wants a word.
S1.quote: I'm not against the machines, I'm against people getting dumped.
S1.fieldNote: Victor's centre outlook shows in his wish for a sensible middle path. True to his steady nature, he would learn the new kit, but only after a colleague has gone first. Taking over paperwork the bosses dislike is a shrewd, low-risk move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next three end with the same thing, full AGI. The difference is how long there is to see it coming. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone, and the government has to keep people afloat while it settles. I don't usually go for big schemes, but you can't have half the country with no wage. I'd say that to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'm finished at Lowfield inside a year. If the machines can drive the harvester and the AI can do the records, the Kemps don't need a junior who's still learning. And the house is gone, the whole plan we've had since we were twenty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, Marta and I would stop looking at houses and put the deposit into a pot to live on. I'd look for anything that's still going locally, maybe the potato packhouse in Brampton or the machinery dealer, while they're still hiring humans. If it got bad, we'd move in with her parents, which neither of us wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gutted. And worried, the kind that wakes you at four and doesn't let you back to sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Marta the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we've still got each other and five months in the bank. Then I'd probably say, sorry about the house. She'd tell me off for saying sorry, she always does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't usually go for big schemes, but here you would. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I think. In normal times I'd say stand on your own feet. But if the ground goes from under everyone at once, there's no feet to stand on. That's not left or right, that's just maths.

S2.say: I'd say this is too fast for anyone and the government has to keep people afloat while it settles. I don't usually back big schemes, but half the country can't be without a wage.
S2.think: I'd be finished at the farm within a year, because machines could drive the harvester and AI could do the records. The house plan we've had since we were twenty-five would be gone.
S2.do: Stops house hunting and turns the deposit into living money with his partner. Looks for any remaining local work at the potato packhouse or machinery dealer, and moves in with her parents if things get bad.
S2.feel: Gutted and worried enough to wake at four in the morning.
S2.quote: If the ground goes from under everyone at once, there's no feet to stand on. That's not left or right, that's just maths.
S2.fieldNote: The loss of the house plan hits Victor harder than the job itself. When I pointed out his shift toward big government schemes, he explained it neatly as maths, not politics. His first instinct is to look locally for any job still done by people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point again, but with five years. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for people to make a plan, but they need to be told straight what's coming. No dressing it up. I'd want the government and the farming bodies to say clearly which jobs go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is tight but doable for me. I'd watch what other people do first, see who lands on their feet, and copy the ones that work. That's how I've always done it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd hold off on the house but keep saving. My cousin Leo already does drone spraying for contractors, so once I'd seen how he got on, I'd probably go for the same licence and work with him. I'd use the AI properly to study for it, because Leo says that's how he passed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but there's a bit of a plan in it, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Leo's line of work goes too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be doing what everyone else is doing, which is looking. But I'd have five years of savings instead of five months. It's not great, but it's better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Lowfield would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete, who does the cattle. He's fifty-two and he's never done anything else. He'd be fine for a year or two, the cattle side's slower to change, but after that I don't know.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to plan, but people need to be told straight which jobs go first. I'd want the government and farming bodies to be clear about it.
S3.think: Five years is tight but doable for me if I watch who lands on their feet and copy them. That's how I've always done things.
S3.do: Keeps saving but holds off on the house. Follows his cousin into drone spraying by getting the same licence, studying with AI tools as his cousin did.
S3.feel: Anxious, but steadier because there's a plan.
S3.quote: I'd watch what other people do first, see who lands on their feet, and copy the ones that work.
S3.fieldNote: Victor's strategy is openly to follow proven paths, and his cousin gives him a ready one. Even so, he knows drone spraying may not last and counts on savings as the real buffer. He thought of an older colleague as the person most at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one, with the most warning. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair run-up and nobody can say they weren't warned. Schools and colleges should be changing what they teach now. I'd say that sort of thing at the pub and probably get argued with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel all right. I'd be thirty-seven when it lands, which isn't young but isn't old, and I'd have a decade to get ready. My worry's more what my kids would do, if we have them by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house after all, but a cheaper one, and pay the mortgage down hard. I'd do the drone licence or something like it in a few years, once it's clear which jobs are holding up. And I'd keep working at Lowfield, because ten years of wages is ten years of wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. It feels far enough away to plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy the house here, when you'd hold off in the others?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because ten years is long enough to pay a chunk off. With two or five I'd be scared of owing money with no job. With ten, I'd want somewhere that's ours before it all changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids, if you had them by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn to do something with people, I think. Teaching, nursing, something where you need a face. Marta says that's what she'd say too, and she sees what the kids are like with the tablets at school.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a fair run-up and nobody can claim they weren't warned, so schools and colleges should start changing what they teach now.
S4.think: I'd feel all right, since I'd be thirty-seven with a decade to prepare. My worry is more about what any children we might have would do.
S4.do: Buys a cheaper house and pays the mortgage down hard while working on at the farm. Takes a drone licence or similar after a few years, once it's clear which jobs are holding up.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly fine, because it's far enough away to plan for.
S4.quote: With ten, I'd want somewhere that's ours before it all changes.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Victor brings the house plan back but makes it more cautious. His reasoning about debt across the three timelines was clear and consistent. His worry moves from himself to children he doesn't have yet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It'd take the house and the job in one go, and I wouldn't have time to see what works for others. What would help is a wage top-up while people find their feet, and plain information about which jobs are safe for a few years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what we'd eat. If robots grow everything cheaper, fine, but I'd want to know someone's still checking it. I've seen what comes out of the bottom of a potato store. You need somebody who cares.

headlineQuote: I've seen what comes out of the bottom of a potato store. You need somebody who cares.
portrait: Victor Santos is a 27-year-old junior worker at Lowfield, a potato, onion and beef finishing farm, where he picks out the stones the optical sorter misses and still drives the harvester too fast. He and his partner Marta, a school teaching assistant, have about five months saved toward a house by their thirtieths. He uses AI now and then and likes to copy what has worked for others before he moves. He stays calm without change, uneasy with steady change, and alarmed by AGI in two years mainly because it would end the house plan. With more warning he would follow his cousin into drone spraying, and with ten years he would buy a cheaper house and pay it down fast.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it would take the house and the job in one go with no time to see what works for others.
whatWouldHelp: A wage top-up while people find their feet and plain information about which jobs are safe for a few years.
